'''Young-Kee Kim''' (born November 25, 1962)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://hep.uchicago.edu/~ykkim/curriculum.shtml |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=hep.uchicago.edu}}</ref> is an American [[physicist]] and the Albert Michelson Distinguished Service Professor of Physics at [[the University of Chicago]] and the Director Emeritus of [[Fermilab|Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]] (Fermilab).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Department of Physics {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physics.uchicago.edu}}</ref> Previously, she served as President of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://www.aps.org/people/young-kee-kim |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250404005554/https://www.aps.org/people/young-kee-kim |archive-date=2025-04-04 |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=www.aps.org |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> Her current work is focused on understanding the origin of mass for [[Elementary particle|fundamental particles]] (the [[Higgs mechanism]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Department of Physics {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physics.uchicago.edu}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Kim was born in Kyeong-Book, South Korea<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://hep.uchicago.edu/~ykkim/curriculum.shtml |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=hep.uchicago.edu}}</ref> and spent her childhood in the countryside.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zierler |first=David |date=January 5, 2021 |title=Oral History Interviews: Young-Kee Kim |url=https://repository.aip.org/node/129631 |journal=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> She received her bachelor’s degree in physics in 1984 and her master’s degree in theoretical particle physics in 1986 from [[Korea University]]. She moved to the United States in 1986 to pursue graduate studies in experimental particle physics at the [[University of Rochester]]. She received a Doctor of Philosophy in physics in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Department of Physics {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physics.uchicago.edu}}</ref>

==Career==
After her Ph.D., Kim joined [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] as a research fellow. She became an assistant professor in 1996, an associate professor in 2000, and a professor of physics in 2002 at [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Department of Physics {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physics.uchicago.edu}}</ref> She moved to the University of Chicago in 2003 and was named the Louis Block Professor of Physics in 2011, the Louis Block Distinguished Service Professor in 2017, and the Albert A. Michelson Distinguished Service Professor in 2024. She also has an appointment at the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] at the University of Chicago.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Enrico Fermi Institute {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://efi.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=efi.uchicago.edu}}</ref> She served as chair of the Department of Physics between 2016 and 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Department of Physics {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physics.uchicago.edu}}</ref> In 2022, she received the Arthur L. Kelly Faculty Prize for Exceptional Service from the University of Chicago.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2022 Arthur L. Kelly Faculty Prize for Exceptional Service in the Physical Sciences Division {{!}} News {{!}} Physical Sciences Division {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physicalsciences.uchicago.edu/news/article/2022-kelly-prize/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physicalsciences.uchicago.edu}}</ref> Kim is the Director Emeritus of Fermilab, after serving as the Interim Director in 2025<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fermilab {{!}} History and Archives {{!}} People |url=https://history.fnal.gov/historical/people/kim_leadership.html |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=history.fnal.gov}}</ref> and as the Deputy Director between 2006 and 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fermilab {{!}} History and Archives {{!}} People |url=https://history.fnal.gov/historical/people/kim_deputy.html |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=history.fnal.gov}}</ref>

== Research ==
As an experimental particle physicist, Kim has devoted much of her research work to understanding the origin of mass for fundamental particles by studying the W boson and the top quark, two of the most massive elementary particles and by studying the [[Higgs boson]] that gives mass to elementary particles.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim {{!}} Department of Physics {{!}} The University of Chicago |url=https://physics.uchicago.edu/people/profile/young-kee-kim/ |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=physics.uchicago.edu}}</ref> She also works in accelerator science, playing a leadership role in NSF's Science and Technology Center, the Center for Bright Beams.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Center for Bright Beams |url=https://cbb.cornell.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Kim started at the AMY experiment at TRISTAN in Japan, then the highest-energy electron-positron collider.<ref>{{Cite web |title=INSPIRE |url=https://inspirehep.net/literature/279829 |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=inspirehep.net}}</ref> There, she studied the properties of [[quantum chromodynamics]], the [[gauge theory]] of the [[Strong interaction|strong nuclear force]], via the properties of jets of particles originating from quarks or gluons.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kim |first=Y. K. |last2=Auchincloss |first2=P. |last3=Blanis |first3=D. |last4=Bodek |first4=A. |last5=Budd |first5=H. |last6=Eno |first6=S. |last7=Fry |first7=C. A. |last8=Harada |first8=H. |last9=Ho |first9=Y. H. |last10=Kumita |first10=T. |last11=Mori |first11=T. |last12=Olsen |first12=S. L. |last13=Shaw |first13=N. M. |last14=Sill |first14=A. |last15=Thorndike |first15=E. H. |date=1989-10-23 |title=Comparison of quark and gluon jets produced in high-energy<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math><mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>e</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">−</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math>annihilations |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.1772 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en-US |volume=63 |issue=17 |pages=1772–1775 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.1772 |issn=0031-9007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221110000457/https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.1772 |archive-date=2022-11-10 |access-date=2026-02-11 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

She subsequently moved to the CDF experiment at the Tevatron in the U.S., which at the time was the highest-energy hadron collider. Kim served as co-spokesperson of the CDF experiment between 2004 and 2006.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://www.aps.org/people/young-kee-kim |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250404005554/https://www.aps.org/people/young-kee-kim |archive-date=2025-04-04 |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=www.aps.org |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2009, she moved to the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://hep.uchicago.edu/~ykkim/research/index.shtml |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=hep.uchicago.edu}}</ref> the current highest-energy hadron collider, to study the origin of mass for fundamental particles (the Higgs mechanism). Kim’s research group has led precise measurements of both the ''W'' and top-quark masses predicting the Higgs boson mass, and subsequently the Higgs’s decay properties (the Higgs boson decaying into two bottom quarks and into two dark matter particles) and potential (via production of two or three Higgs bosons).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://hep.uchicago.edu/~ykkim/research/index.shtml |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=hep.uchicago.edu}}</ref> 

In addition, Kim has been exploiting novel concepts in accelerator science and technology, studying limitations affecting the acceleration and intensity of particle beams at a fundamental level, and developing new approaches, including AI, to overcome these limitations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://hep.uchicago.edu/~ykkim/research/index.shtml |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=hep.uchicago.edu}}</ref>

==Research Leaderships==
*1993–1999: Leader, CDF W Mass Analysis Group
*1995–1996: Co-Leader, CDF Electroweak Physics Group
*2000: Associate Project Manager, CDF Run II Upgrade
*2001: Associate Head, CDF Run II Detector Operations
*2002: Co-Leader, CDF Level-3 Trigger System
*2003–2004: Co-Leader, CDF Top Mass Analysis Group
*2004–2006: Co-Spokesperson, CDF Collaboration at the Tevatron proton-antiproton collider at Fermilab<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young-Kee Kim |url=https://hep.uchicago.edu/~ykkim/research/index.shtml |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=hep.uchicago.edu}}</ref>
*2013-Present: Theme Leader, Center for Bright Beams (NSF's Science and Technology Center)<ref>{{Cite web |title=People {{!}} The Center for Bright Beams |url=https://cbb.cornell.edu/about/people?person-category-tid=20 |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=cbb.cornell.edu}}</ref>
